newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian reformist opposition sets governing steps.
newsitem.headline: Romanian reformist opposition sets governing steps.

text.p: The two main opposition groups which emerged victorious in Romania's general elections on Thursday pledged urgent -- and probably costly -- measures to accelerate market reforms.

A pact signed by the Democratic Convention (CDR) and Social Democrats (USD) called for improved social benefits as well as tighter monetary and fiscal policy after ousting President Ion Ilescu's ruling party of ex-Communists in last Sunday's polls.
But analysts said the incoming government will probably have to temper or abandon some of its more expensive promises to win international support.

The main aim of the pact was to pledge support to CDR leader Emil Constantinescu in the run-off for presidency on November 17. He trailed Iliescu in the first round of the presidential vote, also last Sunday.

It also blended the campaign manifestos of the parties into a joint government programme over the next six months to "stop economic decline, ensure the development of a sound economy and meet Romanians' basic needs".
The measures included pledges to help those worst hit by market reforms, including tax cuts, higher pensions and soft loans for farmers and housing for young couples.

They also tackled some of the complaints of Western institutions, like the International Monetary Fund, by pledging to liberalise currency markets, limit the budget deficit and speed up privatisation. The IMF suspended credits this year after expressing reservations over reforms.
Special mention was made in the programme of the need to avoid a repetition of the energy crunch that shut down large sections of Romanian industry last winter.
Romania's reforms, far behind those in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, are hobbled by rising inflation, now at an annual rate of 45 percent, and high trade and budget deficits.
The leu currency is being artificially propped on the interbank market at a rate 30 percent higher than retail prices, now near 4,500 to the dollar.
Analysts said the outgoing government of Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu had delayed the restructuring of communist-era industry and maintained unemployment at low levels.
